# How 1M+ view long-form videos in this niche are scripted (bench-structure)

Transcripts and metadata are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-structure/txt/<ID>.txt` and `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-structure/meta.txt`. Words per minute (WPM) come from auto-subs, so they are approximate.

## The 8 videos (all 1M+ views, uploaded Nov 2024 – Sep 2026)
| ID | Title (channel, subs) | Views | Length | WPM | Views per sub | Format |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## First 60 seconds (exact auto-sub text)
- **GeoMap:** "What if I told you there's a river in the Amazon that literally cooks anything alive that falls into it? I'm talking about water so hot it reaches 200° F… flowing for 4 miles through the jungle, 400 m from the nearest volcano. Scientists thought this was just a myth until one brave geologist risked his life to prove it exists. But that's just the beginning. Did you know there's an entire continent twice the size of India hiding beneath the Pacific Ocean? I'm about to blow your mind with 50 geography facts…" Then a subscribe ask at 0:43, "Let's dive right in", and **"Fact one, the river of death" at 0:48.**
- **Cleo:** "…That hole is deeper than the deepest part of the ocean. It's deeper than Mount Everest is tall. They started digging it in the 1970s as part of basically a space race, but down… But, what if you just kept digging? If you dug a hole all the way to the center of the Earth, what would you find? What would happen to you?" The promise is stated at 0:30.
- **BeyondTheBlue:** "Imagine you're going down to the bottom of the ocean in a… nuclear submarine. You might think all you'd see is some giant squids or maybe just a completely black void. But what you'd actually see is the walls of the submarine completely closing in on you and crushing you to death… So, what actually exists in the deepest place on Earth?" Promise at 0:45.
- **Curiosity Dude (teaser stack):** "Number three… was chosen by fugitives… Island number four is surrounded by the greatest concentration of sharks on Earth, and the only way onto the island is up a metal ladder bolted to a vertical cliff… Number six is literally called Disappointment Island. And once you hear what happened to the shipwreck survivors… the name starts to make perfect sense. Number eight has been landed on only twice… And the final island has no confirmed human landing… But first, let's start with number one." That is 1:01.
- **Geoff:** "Western Australia is… roughly the size of Western Europe… So, why don't more Australians live in Western Australia if it's basically closer to everything? I'm Jeff, and this is the weird geographic story of Western Australia. The first reason…" Content starts at 0:32.
- **Map Pack:** "most of the facts you learned in geography class… are just straight up wrong. For example, did you know that most penguins actually live in a desert or that there's a mountain taller than Mount Everest?… Number 50…" Content starts at 0:16.
- **Paintify:** the first words are "Mariana Trench." It runs in short, punchy sentences with no intro ("…Something is moving down there.").
- **thePOV:** the slowest open ("hello and welcome to…"). It is saved at 0:25 by "number one is probably the strangest landscape in the entire world."

**What they share:** content starts by 0:48 at the latest (median about 0:30). The title promise is restated within 15–45 s. At least two concrete numbers appear in the first 15 s. No video has a real channel intro.

## Open loops and re-hooks
- **Cleo:**
  - 2:40 "But the craziest part is this deepest hole… is only 0.2% of the way to the center"
  - 4:01 "But, hang on. How do we know that?"
  - 6:05 "But, this gets weirder."
  - 7:38 "And then, you hit something."
  - 8:12 "what's even stranger"
  - 9:30 open questions
  - Result: a turn every ~80 s and a new layer every 2–3 min (mantle 2:58, outer core 5:50, inner core 7:41, center 9:14).
- **BeyondTheBlue:**
  - 1:19 "Everyone assumes the giant squid lives at the absolute bottom… They don't."
  - 1:49 "But the Mariana Trench isn't the ocean floor."
  - 3:24 "That number sounds impressive, but it doesn't really mean anything until you visualize it. Imagine an adult African elephant… on your thumb"
  - 4:42 "I won't just make up crazy stories like Megalodon… to get you to watch" (sets up a question that is answered at 21:38)
  - 9:57 "Unfortunately, it's not a good thing" (plastic found in the trench, at 45% of the video)
  - 14:38 "Even weirder, they are highly toxic"
  - 17:13 "the trench was not silent. It was horrifying."
  - 17:28 "But the craziest part is that they could literally hear the weather" (78%)
  - Result: a turn roughly every 100 s.
- **Geoff:**
  - 2:53 "But what makes Western Australia such an otherwise barren place?"
  - 9:25 "probably the biggest twist in the Western Australian story" (61%)
  - 10:29 "why has Australia still not been able to fully settle…?"
- **Curiosity Dude:** the teasers between 0:15 and 0:58 set up 5 questions. They are answered at 5:59, 8:07, 12:16, 16:42 and 19:03.

## Section structure and escalation
- **GeoMap:** fact 1 gets 47 s, facts 2–10 about 34 s each, facts 10–50 about 22 s each. The best fact is played long at the start, then the pace speeds up.
- **thePOV:** items run 1:06–2:17, and #1 gets 3:40, the longest. It then adds a "one final bonus" twist at 17:03.
- **Curiosity Dude:** 2:00–2:40 per item. The last item is the strongest possible ending ("no human has ever set foot").
- **Map Pack:** flat ~36 s per item and a weak #1 (Afghanistan isn't in the Middle East). It has the lowest views-per-sub of the list videos.
- **Cleo and BeyondTheBlue:** the physical descent works as a built-in progress bar. Every level is deeper, hotter or stranger, so the story climbs without extra effort.
- **Geoff:** environment, then deep time (3.8 bn-year rock, 4.4 bn-year zircons), then history, then the twist, then economics, then a one-line answer ("is simple…").

## How numbers are framed
- **Two anchors:** "deeper than the deepest part of the ocean… deeper than Everest is tall"; "twice the size of India"; "Russia… larger than Pluto's entire surface"; "33 states… each have a larger population."
- **Tiny-fraction reveal:** "only 0.2% of the way."
- **Body scale:** "elephant on your thumb… every square inch."
- **US units first** (°F, miles, ft).

## Endings
- **Best:**
  - Cleo: no call to action, just open questions and a wonder line ("We are a curious species, locked on the outside of our own home…").
  - BeyondTheBlue: answers the megalodon question raised at 4:42, then points to the related video.
  - Paintify: stops on its eeriest line, with no outro.
- **Weak:** Map Pack's generic thanks, Curiosity Dude's plea to the algorithm, Geoff's sponsor at 14:52.

# Blueprint for a 10–14 minute script
Target about 1,850 words at 150–160 WPM (ElevenLabs deep male voice). That gives 7 sections plus the finale.

## 0:00–0:60
| Time | Beat | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 s | **Impossible-sounding true fact** with a number and a visual anchor | 18 words max; the visual is already moving (globe zoom) |
| 5–12 s | Two hard specifics (place, number, year), then the brand line "Sounds fake. It's 100% real." | No adjectives without numbers |
| 12–20 s | **Flip the misconception:** "You'd think… But…" or "Everyone assumes X. They don't." | |
| 20–30 s | **Promise = the title question, word for word**, plus the end state ("by the end you'll see why…") | |
| 30–50 s | **Teaser stack:** 3 future beats, each one concrete strange detail left unexplained; the last one is the finale ("And the last one… no human has ever…") | Each teased beat must actually come later |
| 50–60 s | One clause of credibility (a named source: NASA GRACE, USGS, a 2023 *Nature* paper), then a hard cut into section 1 | No "let's dive in", no subscribe ask |

## Section template (75–110 s; the finale gets about 2:30)
1. **0–5 s, label line:** "the X that Y" ("the river of death", "the country bigger than Pluto").
2. **5–40 s:** setup, the core fact, and a scale anchor (two anchors or body scale).
3. **40–60 s, the turn:** "But here's the part that doesn't make sense…" or "Hang on. How do we know that?", followed by evidence (map overlay, satellite image, data chart).
4. **60–80 s:** the payoff or twist.
5. **80–90 s, bridge:** close this question and open the next one in the same breath ("…and that's nothing compared to what's under Antarctica.").

**Pacing rules:**
- A small re-hook every 30–45 s (a "but", a question, or a number reveal).
- A section or level change every 90–120 s.
- A change of visual mode every ~2 min (globe, map, chart, public-domain photo) with a sound hit.
- Call back to the teasers at about 25%, 50% and 75%.

## Escalation ladder
| Position | Section |
|---|---|
| S1 | **2nd-strongest** item: pays off the cold open within 2 min |
| S2–S3 | Scale shocks |
| S4 (~35–40%) | "How do we know?" beat on method and evidence (Cleo 4:01) |
| S5 (~45–50%) | Human stakes / gut-punch (BeyondTheBlue 9:57) |
| S6 (~60–65%) | **"Biggest twist":** reframes an earlier section (Geoff 9:25) |
| S7 (~75–80%) | "But the craziest part…" sensory wow moment (BeyondTheBlue 17:28) |
| Finale (85–97%) | The strongest and longest section; answers the cold-open question |

## Ending (last 30–40 s)
1. Answer the main question.
2. One line on what is still unknown.
3. A wonder line people can quote.
4. A comment prompt of 10 s or less that names 2 items ("Which one sounded the most fake?").
5. End screen pointing to one specific video.

Stop there, with no thank-you ramble.

## Phrases that work (all seen in the transcripts)
- "What if I told you…" / "But that's just the beginning."
- "That number sounds impressive, but it doesn't really mean anything until you visualize it. Imagine…"
- "But, hang on. How do we know that?" / "But, this gets weirder." / "And then, you hit something."
- "But the craziest part is…" / "Even weirder…" / "…the biggest twist in the story."
- "Everyone assumes X. They don't."
- "Number six is literally called Disappointment Island. And once you hear what happened… the name starts to make perfect sense."
- "I won't just make up crazy stories… to get you to watch." Trust used as the hook fits a myth-busting brand.

## What kills retention
- Opening with "hello and welcome to…", or any channel intro longer than one line.
- A subscribe ask before the first payoff (GeoMap 0:43).
- Sponsor or self-promo breaks in the first 3 min (Geoff mentions his other channel at 2:21).
- A flat list where every item gets the same time, or a weak #1 (Map Pack).
- Vague claims like "scientists can't explain" with no specific behind them.
- Making things up. Paintify's views rest on unverifiable claims (an upright-walking chimp found in 2012, radio pulses from the Gamburtsev Mountains in 2013). That breaks our facts-only rule and invites a backlash in the comments.
- Long outros or pleas to the algorithm.
- Teasing an item and never paying it off.

## Long-form 1M+ benchmark (packaging side): what it takes in the "weird Earth / myths" niche

**Data base:** 50 search queries plus the upload lists of 18 channels gave 1,461 long-form (6 min or longer) videos with 1M+ views. Of these, 96 are outliers: views at least 10x the channel's subscribers, or a channel under 300K subs. Saved under `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-packaging/` (`all_rows2.json`, `q_all.json`, `q_more.json`, `sheet1.jpg`, `sheet2.jpg`).

### (a) Top outliers (topic and packaging power, not channel power)

| Title | Views | Subs | x subs | Len | Age |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 Geography Facts So Crazy They'll Change How You See the World (GeoMap Unveiled) | 5.6M | 48K | 119x (2,090x channel median) | 22m | 17mo |
| 50 Facts About Texas That Sound Fake But Are 100% True (Geography Explored) | 1.9M | 14K | 134x | 73m | 8mo |
| Unseen Drone & Satellite Images of North Sentinel Island | 4.4M | 8K | 576x | 8m | 8y |
| Wildest Borders Around The World (Data World) | 2.1M | 26K | 83x | 10m | 17mo |
| Mariana Trench: What They Found In The Deepest Place On Earth (Uncharted Depths) | 4.1M | 34K | 122x | 18m | 8mo |
| Every Unexplored Place on Earth (Paintify) | 1.6M | 22K | 73x | 12m | 8mo |
| The Most Impossible to Reach Islands on Google Earth (Curiosity Dude) | 2.5M | 38K | 67x | 21m | 5mo |
| Why Deep Sea Creatures Get Creepier the Deeper You Go (Mr. Science) | 17.2M | 265K | 65x | 18m | 12mo |
| This Discovery in the Mariana Trench Will Transform Geopolitics (New Nature) | 12.5M | 234K | 54x | 28m | 16mo |
| What They Found In the Deepest Place on Earth (Astrum Earth) | 13.2M | 503K | 26x | 35m | 15mo |
| When Antarctica Was a Jungle (Mr. Science) | 5.3M | 265K | 20x | 26m | **2.5mo** |
| Why There is No Bridge Between Europe and Africa (Map Pack) | 7.1M | 442K | 16x (62x median) | 33m | 3y |
| Why Nobody Stays in Alaska (It's Not the Cold) (Map Pack) | 5.8M | 442K | 13x | 37m | 21mo |
| 10 Scientifically Impossible Places That Actually Exist (Mind Boggler) | 38.8M | 2.9M | 13x | 11m | 7y |
| Weirdest Places On Earth Explained (Professor Why) | 1.6M | 4K | 414x | 6m | 5mo |

Small faceless channels (4K–50K subs) are still producing 1M+ long-form videos in 2025–26. But it is hit-driven: GeoMap Unveiled's median video gets 2.7K views and Geography Explored's gets 4.4K. Each had 1 hit in roughly 40 uploads, so topic plus packaging decides it, not the channel.

### (b) Title formulas that win

Outlier titles have a median of 51 characters and 8–9 words. The niche as a whole is 45 characters. Keep to 45–60 characters so it isn't cut off on mobile.

1. **Number + "sound fake but true"** (our channel's own tagline): "50 Facts About Texas That Sound Fake But Are 100% True" (54 characters). "50 Geography Facts That Are Fake (But You Believed Them)" got 2.5M and 2.9M in two versions.
2. **"Why + paradox + (It's Not the obvious)":** "Why Nobody Stays in Alaska (It's Not the Cold)" (46). "Real Reason Ships Don't Pass Under South America (It's Not the Distance)" (72, 4.3M). The bracket cancels the obvious answer, which creates a curiosity gap. This pattern is 8% of outlier titles vs 2% of the niche.
3. **"What They Found in [superlative place]":** "What They Found In the Deepest Place on Earth" (45, 13.2M).
4. **"Every [category] on Earth":** "Every Unexplored Place on Earth" (31). It promises completeness.
5. **"Nothing About X Is Normal... Here's Why"** / **"Why X Gets [weirder] the Deeper You Go"** (53–56).
6. **Time-reversal:** "When Antarctica Was a Jungle" (28 characters, 5.3M in 10 weeks).

**Word signals in outlier titles vs the niche:**
- superlative "Most/-est": 38% vs 25%
- "Earth/World": 33% vs 20%
- one ALL-CAPS word ("NOBODY", "NOT"): 24% vs 13%
- "Impossible / Shouldn't Exist / Doesn't Add Up": 9% vs 3%

Plain "How…" and question marks under-index.

**"(No AI)" tags:** they now appear on several 1M+ titles. We may not use the tag (we never mention AI). Instead we should signal authenticity with "real satellite data" or "NASA images".

### (c) Duration sweet spot
- All 1M+ niche long-form: median 17.8 min.
- Explainer-type outliers (excluding 4K stock compilations): median **20.5 min**, interquartile range 15–30 min. 2025–26 uploads: median 21.8 min.
- The 45–190 min "4K travel documentary" compilations depend on stock footage, which we can't use, so they are not reproducible for us.
- The 6–10 min hits are mostly 2016–2019 RealLifeLore/Vox legacy.
- **Target: 16–22 min.** A "50 facts" list format can stretch to 25–30 min.

### (d) Thumbnail rules (from 20 outlier thumbnails viewed)
- **0–4 words**, usually 2–3, as heavy condensed sans-serif in white on black boxes, with **one word in red** ("CAN'T **EXPLAIN**", "WHAT **CHINA** FOUND", "IT'S **TERRIFYING**", "**ONLY** 8 MILES").
- Thumbnail text **adds to the title, never repeats it**. Example: title "No Bridge Between Europe and Africa", thumbnail "ONLY 8 MILES".
- **No presenter faces at all.** The only people are documentary subjects (Sentinelese).
- **Maps dominate the geography winners:** satellite or relief terrain with the target region as an extruded, flat-colour slab with a drop shadow (Texas blue, Alaska navy, Australia yellow with red density). Each has **one white curved arrow** to a red pin or glow. A **flag** is an instant identifier.
- **Circles:** a yellow ring around a tiny object (a creature in a trench), or a red dashed border line.
- **Scale contrast:** a tiny diver next to a huge creature, a tiny rock in an empty ocean ("NO HUMAN HAS EVER BEEN HERE"), a tiny sub in the abyss.
- **Palette:** deep navy/teal and black for deep sea and ice, saturated green-brown terrain, with red and yellow as the only accents.
- **Cutaways** (mountain, ice sheet and lava cross-section plus a flag) work for "under X" topics. These are reproducible in Three.js.
- **Grid of 6 labelled tiles** for "Every X" catalogue videos (Paintify, Professor Why).
- Several outliers use generated art. We must hit the same look with real NASA/USGS imagery and 3D renders.

### (e) Topic archetypes: proven vs saturated (1M+ count / count since May 2025)

**Saturated (avoid as a head-on topic):**
- Mariana Trench / deepest place: 11 / **9**, with a new 1M+ video almost monthly.
- Forbidden / impossible-to-reach places: 18 / 11, plus a Paint Explainer series.
- North Sentinel: 14 / 5.
- Antarctica's hidden secrets: 12 / 7.
- Deepest hole / Kola: 11, with a 48M incumbent.
- "Why nobody lives in X": 67 / 12; Geography By Geoff posts it weekly.

**Proven but under-supplied recently (gaps):**
- **"Facts that sound fake but are true" mega-lists:** a 48K-sub and a 14K-sub channel both broke out, and this is exactly the Myth Juice brand.
- **Strange borders / enclaves / countries that don't exist:** 39 total but only 8 recent. "Enclaves and exclaves explained" has 0 long-form videos at 100K+, while Data World got 2.1M on 26K subs. Our best Short was "Countries Split in Two".
- **Deep-time "When X was Y":** 9 / 1. Mr. Science got 5.3M in 10 weeks.
- **Maps are wrong / projection:** 25.7M and 23.8M incumbents are 9–10 years old, with only 2 recent.
- **Time zones / date line:** 5 / 0.
- **Earth stopped spinning / hypotheticals:** 31 / 0 recent; all incumbents are old.
- **Lost continents / Zealandia:** 4 / 1.

### (f) 10 packaging rules for a 1M-view video here
1. Pick a topic with proven 1M+ demand but **fewer than 2 strong uploads in the last 12 months**. Avoid the saturated list in (e).
2. The topic must sound false on first read. "Sounds fake but is 100% true" is the strongest small-channel formula found.
3. Title: 45–60 characters, 8–10 words, a superlative or "Earth/World", at most one ALL-CAPS word, and an **"(It's Not X)" or "Actually" reversal**.
4. Thumbnail: 2–4 words that **complete** the title, white on black boxes with one red word, and no face.
5. The thumbnail hero is a **3D relief or satellite map** with one flat-coloured extruded region, one white arrow and one red pin or ring. For "under" topics, use a cutaway cross-section.
6. Build in scale contrast: a tiny human or object against something huge.
7. Length 16–22 min. A "50 facts" list can run 25–30 min with numbered chapters to hold retention.
8. Signal authenticity on screen and in the description: real NASA/USGS satellite and elevation data. The audience is rewarding "real" over generated imagery.
9. Plan a series from day one ("Part 2", "Every X"). Paintify, Paint Explainer and Map Pack each got repeat 1M+ videos from one format.
10. Use the channel's own Shorts as a test bed. Turn the top Short angle ("countries split in two") into the long-form and package it the same way. A/B test 3 thumbnails with "Test & Compare".

# Visual grammar of million-view geography long-form videos, translated into our production rules

## 1. Benchmark (10 storyboards, about 1 frame every 10 s, all contact sheets viewed)

Contact sheets and thumbnails are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-visual/sb/` (`sheet_<ID>.jpg`) and `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-visual/th/thumbs.jpg`. The metric script is `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-juicytea-media/4a181100-5b6b-5601-bf64-5ea13c092764/scratchpad/research/bench-visual-scripts/metrics.py`.

## 2. What the winners share

1. **Nothing is ever static.** The median is about 5 s per visual change. Map-heavy videos hold a shot for 4–5.5 s because labels, highlights and camera moves keep happening inside it. Footage-heavy videos cut faster (Wendover 2.6 s).
2. **One base-map look carries 40–85% of the runtime.** Each channel has a single map style it returns to:
   - RealLifeLore: black ocean, darkened satellite land, one orange-red glowing country.
   - Atlas Pro: elevation-coloured relief with shaded water depth.
   - Map Pack: a flat satellite map.
   - Scary Interesting: cream paper with red routes.
3. **Highlighting works one way everywhere.** The target is filled with a saturated colour and an outer glow, with a thin white outline. Everything else is dimmed.
4. **On-screen text is sparse.** It is limited to place labels (caps, small pill or leader line), numbers (heights, areas, depths, years), segment headers (Map Pack's "FACT 37 – OTTAWA, CANADA") and numbered chapter cards. **None of the 10 videos burn in subtitles.**
5. **Scale comparisons follow a few patterns:**
   - Drag a true-shape outline over the viewer's home turf (RealLifeLore puts Australia over the USA at 0:29).
   - Side-by-side shapes with square-mile labels (Map Pack: Madagascar vs Britain, Greenland vs Africa).
   - Height diagrams with numbers (Everest).
   - A live depth counter plus a vertical ruler (Kurzgesagt, "10,929 m").
6. **Motion graphics live inside the map:**
   - curved migration arcs
   - cyan ocean-current arrows
   - a dashed route ending in a red skull (Scary Interesting thumbnail)
   - pulse markers
   - glowing data-dot densities (Johnny Harris)
7. **Inserts are graded to match the map.** Archival material is turned sepia or teal with grain, placed in rounded photo-print frames with drop shadows, or shown as newspaper headlines, documents and blueprints.
8. **The first 30 seconds follow a pattern:**
   - The first frame is never a title. It is a moving establishing shot (aerial or map).
   - The subject is highlighted by about 10 s.
   - A scale comparison or a shocking number arrives by about 30 s.
   - The title sting comes at 0:34–1:08, or there is none at all.
9. **Thumbnails** use one map or globe hero with a single saturated highlight, a yellow arrow or circle, and 4 words or fewer ("YOU'VE BEEN LIED TO", "WHY EVERYBODY LIVES IN RED"). Some use no text: a dark globe with a red route and a skull.

**Proof that our setup can work:** Atlas Pro's Ice Age video (6M views, about 80% elevation maps), Map Pack (2.5M, about 85% one flat map) and Scary Interesting (PD art plus paper maps) are all faceless and could be produced programmatically. The footage share in RealLifeLore and Wendover we replace with NASA/NOAA public-domain video (ISS time-lapses, NASA SVS visualisations, NOAA Ocean Exploration footage) and Ken Burns moves on PD photos.

## 3. Production style guide for our video

### Format
- 1920x1080 at 30 fps.
- Render raw RGB frames and pipe them to ffmpeg: `-f rawvideo -pix_fmt rgb24 -s 1920x1080 -r 30 -i -`, then x264 at CRF 16, yuv420p, tagged BT.709.
- Optionally upscale the master to 2560x1440 for upload. That makes YouTube use its higher-quality VP9 encode, so grain and gradients survive.
- Keep key information out of the bottom 12% of the frame. Reserve the last 20 s for the end-screen layout.

### Cut cadence
- **0:00–1:00:** a visual event (cut, label, highlight, counter or camera change) every 2–3 s.
- **After the first minute:** an event every 3–5 s, a hard cut every 5–7 s on average, and no shot longer than 12 s without an internal event.
- Cuts and highlights land on ElevenLabs word timestamps. Highlights pop 2–4 frames before the key word.
- **Rhythm:** a map sequence of 15–40 s with 4–8 events, then 2–3 inserts of 3–4 s each (PD photo or video), then back to the map. A chapter card every 2–4 min, held for 3 s, with a big number and a 2–4 word title.
- **Opening template:**
  - 0–3 s: the globe is already rotating, with the claim.
  - 3–8 s: zoom from space down to the place while the outline draws on.
  - 8–15 s: glowing highlight plus a counter.
  - 15–30 s: true-size overlay on the USA.
  - 30–40 s: a "but…" twist and a 3-cut montage.
  - Title sting of 2 s, no later than 0:40.

### Camera rules
- Every frame moves. Stills get at least 1.5–3% scale drift or a 20–40 px pan per 10 s. All moves use cubic or exponential easing, never linear.
- **Zoom from space to place:**
  - Interpolate log(altitude) over 3–5 s.
  - Tilt from 0° to 35–45° on arrival, with the last 30% eased out.
  - Hold at least 1.5 s before the next label.
- Travelling east means moving screen-right. Never reverse a zoom within the same shot.
- **Parallax:** the label layer moves at 1.15x the map; the cloud layer at 1.3x.
- **Whip transitions** between distant places: 6–8 frames, with motion blur from averaging 4 sub-frames (only on these shots).
- **Match-cut:** zoom into a map point, then dissolve into a photo of the same spot.

### Palette
| Use | Colour |
|---|---|
| Space | #05070D |
| Deep ocean to shelf | #0A1A2E to #12385A |
| Land | Blue Marble, 30% desaturated, 15% darker (elevation tint for terrain chapters) |
| Hero highlight | #FF5A36, with glow |
| Water, routes, data | #3DE3FF |
| Arrows and circles (match the thumbnail) | #FFD23F |
| Primary label | #F4F6FA |
| Secondary label | #9AA7B8 |
| Archival split-tone | shadows #0E2A33, highlights #E8DCC0 |

One shared colour-grade lookup table (.cube): teal shadows, warm highlights, contrast +8%.

### Typography (all free Google Fonts)
| Use | Font and treatment |
|---|---|
| Labels | Barlow Condensed SemiBold, all caps, +8% tracking, 30–38 px, on a 70% black pill or with a leader line and dot |
| Counters | Inter Bold with tabular figures, 96–180 px, units at 50% size |
| Hook words and chapter cards | Bebas Neue, 180–260 px. Animate from 108% to 100% scale with a 6-frame blur-in; accent word in orange |
| Dates on archival inserts | Special Elite |

Limits: at most 2 text elements on screen, at most 7 words each, no subtitles.

### Premium finishing (all cheap)
- **Bloom:** blur the highlight layer at quarter resolution (σ 8–20) and add it at 35–60%.
- **Vignette:** 15–25% (`vignette=PI/5`).
- **Grain:** `noise=alls=5:allf=t` normally; strength 10 on archival.
- **Depth of field:** tilt-shift blur on the top and bottom 20% of tilted maps; blur the background behind text cards.
- **Light leaks:** procedural warm radial gradients at 10–20% opacity, on transitions and archival only.
- **Globe atmosphere:** rim glow #6FC3FF and a star field.
- **Archival look:** rounded print frames, 30 px shadow, dust overlay, ±1 px gate weave.

### Sound design per visual device
| Visual device | Sound cue |
|---|---|
| Zoom from space | Reverse-cymbal riser, then a sub-boom on arrival, over a wind bed |
| Outline draw-on | Soft swish plus a tonal ping |
| Fill or highlight pop | Low thump or pluck |
| Label pop-in | Quiet UI tick (about -24 dB) |
| Counter | Ticks matched to the count rate, ending in a ding or impact |
| Route or arrow | Pen scratch or a whoosh scaled to the line's length |
| True-size drag | Drag whoosh, then a heavy impact when the shape lands |
| Depth or cross-section | Sonar ping, creaks, a descending drone |
| Archival insert | Projector loop and crackle under the music |
| Chapter card or reveal | Music cuts out 0.5 s before, then a boom and reverse swell |

Use only CC0 sound effects.

## 4. Devices ranked by quality per effort (4-core CPU, no GPU)

| Rank | Device | How to build it | Estimated cost per frame |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Relief or satellite base map** | Pre-render once at 16k px from DEM hillshade with elevation tint, or Blue Marble (21600x10800). Animate with crops and `cv2.warpPerspective` for a 2.5D tilt | about 20–30 ms |
| 2 | **Vector overlays** | Cairo or skia: border draw-on via dash offset, glowing fills, arcs, pulse markers, labels | about 10–30 ms |
| 3 | **True-size comparison** | Reproject the outline to an equal-area projection at each location, then drag it. The single best device for this niche | cheap |
| 4 | **2D globe with simulated 3D (numpy)** | Orthographic lat/lon lookup plus `cv2.remap` on a mipmapped texture. Day/night blend with Black Marble, sun shading, rim glow | about 50–150 ms |
| 5 | **Counters, depth rulers, bars, cross-sections** | Draw elevation or depth profiles taken from real GEBCO/SRTM data | cheap |
| 6 | **PD photos** | Ken Burns moves, grade, grain, print frames | about 15 ms |
| 7 | **NASA/NOAA PD video** | Grade only | almost free |
| 8 | **Three.js WebGL (software renderer)** | DEM terrain flyovers only | about 1–3 s per frame (my estimate) |

Three.js should be limited to hero shots totalling 60 s or less (about 1,800 frames, roughly 30–90 min of rendering).

**Render budget:** a 15-min video is 27,000 frames. At about 0.15 s per frame across 4 workers, that is roughly 20 min of rendering, plus WebGL hero shots.

**Avoid:**
- particles, volumetric clouds and ocean shaders in software WebGL
- capturing frames from a headless browser
- full-resolution Gaussian blur on every frame
- linear moves and static holds
- busy labels
- Sentinel-2 cloudless imagery after 2016, because it is licensed non-commercial (CC BY-NC-SA). Use NASA GIBS imagery through the existing `gibs.py`, or Landsat, instead.

candidates.title: Earth Is NOT Round. Here's Its Real Shape
candidates.premise: Everything we're taught about Earth's shape is a simplification. The planet is a squashed, lumpy 'gravity potato'. The ocean surface has hills and valleys more than 100 m high. 'Sea level' changes from place to place. The solid ground rises and falls every day. The shape is still changing right now. We build it up with a 3D globe that gets stranger section by section.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone 'knows' Earth is a ball and the sea is flat, and everyone has wondered where the highest point really is. Proving both assumptions wrong with real satellite data is the kind of 'wait, WHAT?' that people share. Shorts on this exact idea pull huge numbers: 'Chimborazo is closer to space' 30M, the Indian Ocean 'gravity hole' 4.4M, 'Earth's real shape' 684K.
killer_facts: The summit of Chimborazo (Ecuador) is about 6,384.4 km from Earth's center, more than 2 km farther than Everest's summit. Source: NOAA Ocean Service, 'What is the highest point on Earth as measured from Earth's center?'

Earth's equatorial radius (6,378.137 km) is about 21.4 km larger than its polar radius (6,356.752 km). Surface gravity runs from about 9.780 to 9.832 m/s², so you weigh roughly 0.5% less at the equator. Source: WGS84 ellipsoid and normal-gravity formula (NGA).

South of India the ocean surface sits about 106 m below the reference ellipsoid (the 'Indian Ocean Geoid Low'). Near New Guinea it sits about 85 m above, a swing of about 190 m that nobody can see. Source: Pal & Ghosh, Geophysical Research Letters 2023; EGM2008 geoid (NGA).

The Greenwich meridian line is about 102 m from the GPS zero-longitude line, because local gravity tilts 'straight down'. Source: Malys et al., Journal of Geodesy 2015, 'Why the Greenwich meridian moved'.

The Moon raises the 'solid' ground by tens of cm twice a day. In 1992 CERN found that this tide stretches its 27 km LEP collider ring enough to change the beam energy. Source: CERN, 'LEP and the Moon' (1992); Earth-tide literature.

Land is still rebounding from the last ice age. Sweden's High Coast has risen about 286 m (UNESCO World Heritage listing), and Finland gains roughly 7 km² of land per year (BIFROST GPS network). Satellites saw Earth's flattening trend reverse around 1998 as mass shifted. Source: Cox & Chao, Science 2002.
escalation_arc: Cold open: Everest isn't the point closest to space. Chimborazo wins by 2 km. Why?
Earth is fat: spin speed of 1,670 km/h at the equator, a 21 km bulge, and you weigh less in Quito than in Oslo.
It isn't even a smooth fat ball. The real geoid is a lumpy 'gravity potato' (GOCE/GRACE maps).
The ocean isn't flat. A 106 m 'hole' in the Indian Ocean and an 85 m hill near New Guinea, invisible to sailors.
'Sea level' is a myth. The Panama Canal's oceans sit at different heights, and the Greenwich line is 102 m off GPS zero.
The ground breathes. Earth tides lift your city about 30 cm twice a day, and CERN had to correct for the Moon.
The planet is still springing back from the ice age. Hudson Bay has weak gravity, Sweden rose 286 m, and Finland grows 7 km² a year.
Finale: Earth's shape is changing right now. Satellites watched the bulge's trend flip around 1998 as ice and water moved. The 'globe' is a live map.

A 3D 'ocean surface hill' sheet over GEBCO bathymetry. Animated plumb-line arrows at Greenwich. A pulsing ground-tide animation over a city map (OpenFreeMap). GRACE mass-change time series (NASA PD) and a Landsat comparison of the High Coast shoreline. Data-driven lower-thirds with numbers.

candidates.title: Why Do All the Continents Point South?
candidates.premise: Spin a globe and Earth looks like it's 'dripping'. South America, Africa, India, Greenland, Florida, Baja, Korea and Scandinavia all taper south. Land is crammed into the north and almost never sits opposite other land. One hemisphere is nearly all water. We go through every weird asymmetry in how Earth's land is laid out, bust the myths, and end with where the 'drip' is heading.
candidates.universal_hook: Once you've noticed it, you can't stop seeing it, and almost nobody has heard an explanation. Kids ask whether you can 'dig to China', and adults have never checked. The short 'Why Does Earth Look Drippy?' has 27M views and 'Why do all the continents point south?' has 2.5M, but there's no long-form answer.
killer_facts: Roughly two-thirds (about 68%) of Earth's land and about 88% of its people are in the Northern Hemisphere. Sources: Wikipedia/Britannica 'Northern Hemisphere'; Kummu & Varis, Applied Geography 2011, 'The world by latitudes'.

Only about 15% of land has land on the exact opposite side of the planet, about 4.4% of Earth's surface. Dig straight down from almost anywhere in the US and you surface in the Indian Ocean, not China. Source: Wikipedia 'Antipodes'; reproducible by flipping Natural Earth polygons.

There is a 'water hemisphere' centered near New Zealand's Bounty Islands that is about 89% water. The opposite 'land hemisphere', centered near Nantes, France, holds about 80% of all land. Source: Wikipedia 'Land and water hemispheres'.
The Pacific Ocean (about 165 million km²) is larger than all the land on Earth combined (about 149 million km²). Source: NOAA Ocean Explorer / Ocean Service.

In 1620 Francis Bacon remarked that the Old and New Worlds are 'broad towards the north and pointed towards the south'. People often misquote this as him spotting continental fit. Source: Bacon, Novum Organum (verify the exact aphorism in the Devey translation, Project Gutenberg #45988).

In 1875 William Lowthian Green proposed that Earth was collapsing into a tetrahedron to explain the land/ocean pattern. It was taken seriously for decades until plate tectonics replaced it. Source: Green, 'Vestiges of the Molten Globe' (1875); Wikipedia 'Tetrahedral hypothesis'.
escalation_arc: Hook: spin the globe. Every big landmass drips south. Name 10 of them in 10 seconds.
Myth check: the 'Bacon noticed continental drift' story is wrong. What he really noticed in 1620 was the drip.
The north is crammed: about 68% of land and about 88% of humans on one half of the planet.
Land avoids land: only about 4% of the surface has land opposite land. 'Dig to China' lands you in the ocean.
There's a hemisphere that is 89% water, and the Pacific alone is bigger than all the land.
The 1875 theory that Earth is a tetrahedron, and why serious scientists bought it.
The real story: Gondwana broke apart, the plates rafted north, and Antarctica parked on the pole. Some of the 'drip' is still unexplained.
Finale: the drip is temporary. Plate models show the continents colliding into the next supercontinent, and what your country's spot becomes.

candidates.title: The Ocean Has Its Own Rivers, Lakes and Waterfalls

killer_facts: The Denmark Strait cataract is the largest waterfall on Earth. Cold water drops about 3,505 m (11,500 ft) underwater, carrying about 175 million ft³/s (about 5 million m³/s), roughly 2,000 times Niagara. Source: NOAA Ocean Service, 'What is the largest waterfall?'

The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined, about 100+ Sv offshore against about 1.2 Sv of total river discharge. Sources: NOAA Ocean Service; Dai & Trenberth 2002 for river totals.

In 2010 the University of Leeds found a river flowing along the floor of the Black Sea. At about 22,000 m³/s, about 350 times the Thames, it would be the world's 6th-largest river if it ran on land. Source: University of Leeds / Autosub3 2010; Wikipedia 'Black Sea undersea river'.

The seafloor has brine 'lakes' with shorelines and waves that kill animals that swim in, such as the Gulf of Mexico's 'Jacuzzi of Despair' (2015). More were discovered in the Red Sea in 2020. Sources: NOAA Ocean Exploration; Purkis et al., Communications Earth & Environment 2022.
Internal waves in the Luzon Strait reach about 170 m tall, the biggest waves on Earth, and they move invisibly beneath the surface. Source: Alford et al., Nature 2015.
In the South Pacific Gyre, the ocean's 'desert', scientists revived microbes from seafloor sediment up to 101.5 million years old. Source: Morono et al., Nature Communications 2020 (JAMSTEC/URI).

Lakes under the ocean: brine pools with beaches, waves, and the 'Jacuzzi of Despair'.
The world's biggest waterfall is underwater: a 3.5 km drop and 2,000 Niagaras, off Greenland.

The ocean's desert: the emptiest, clearest water on Earth, where the seafloor grows mm per thousand years.

candidates.title: Most of Earth Has Never Been Mapped. Here's Proof.
candidates.premise: Your phone shows every street on Earth, yet most of the planet's solid surface has never been measured directly. We show the real map of what humanity has actually seen versus what's guessed. We bust the 'better maps of Mars' line (it's true), then go through what turns up every time we look: new mountains, thousands of 'new' islands, places no human has reached. It ends with when the last blank on Earth's map will be filled.
candidates.universal_hook: Every person assumes Google already mapped everything. Finding out that a part of Earth twice the size of all land is still essentially unmeasured feels like discovering a secret.
killer_facts: As of the June 2025 GEBCO grid, only about 27.3% of the seafloor had been mapped to modern standards, up from 6% in 2017. A later Seabed 2030 update reports 28.7%. Source: Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030.
That leaves roughly 260 million km² of unmapped seafloor, close to twice the area of all land on Earth (about 149 million km²). This is computed from Seabed 2030 and NOAA ocean-area figures.

Mars has a global image mosaic at about 5 m per pixel, while most of Earth's seafloor is known only at kilometer scale from satellite gravity. Sources: Caltech Murray Lab Global CTX Mosaic (2023); GEBCO documentation.
In 2023 Japan recounted its islands with modern digital maps: 14,125, not the 6,852 it had used since 1987. Source: Geospatial Information Authority of Japan (February 2023).
In 2024 Schmidt Ocean Institute discovered an undersea mountain about 3,109 m tall off Chile. Source: Schmidt Ocean Institute press release, 2024.
At about 3.2% of the seafloor mapped per year, the full map could be finished in about 20 years. Source: Frontiers in Marine Science 2025, 'Status of global seafloor mapping effort'.

The true coverage map: about 73% blank, an area twice the size of all continents combined.
Myth check: 'we've mapped Mars better than our oceans' is true, and here's the resolution comparison.
What happens when we look: the MH370 search revealed volcanoes and ridges no one knew existed.

Even land was miscounted: Japan suddenly 'found' 7,000 more islands in 2023.
Places still untouched: the highest unclimbed mountain (Gangkhar Puensum, 7,570 m) and caves only found this century.
Finale: the race to finish the last map of Earth within our lifetime.

candidates.title: The Borders So Strange You Can See Them From Space
candidates.premise: Borders are supposed to be invisible lines, yet some are so extreme that astronauts and satellites can see them. These include a glowing line of floodlights, a 6 m cut through forests, a fence that changed a desert's vegetation, and a country that goes dark at night. Each border is visible for a stranger reason than the last, and we bust the most famous 'proof' image along the way.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone has been told 'borders don't exist in nature'. Seeing real satellite proof that they do, and learning why, combines geography, people and history in one image.
killer_facts: The India–Pakistan border is lit by so many floodlights that it shows up from the International Space Station as an orange line. Source: NASA Earth Observatory, 'India-Pakistan Borderlands at Night' (ISS astronaut photo).
Along the US–Canada border (8,891 km), crews keep a 6 m (20 ft) 'vista' clear-cut through forests, visible from the air and in satellite imagery. Source: International Boundary Commission.

The famous green-vs-brown Haiti/Dominican Republic image hides a myth. The '2% forest' figure has no traceable source: satellite analysis puts tree cover around 30%, although primary forest is under 1%. Sources: Wampler et al. 2014 (IJAEOG); Hedges et al., PNAS 2018.

The Israel–Egypt border in the Negev/Sinai shows as a sharp brightness and vegetation line caused by different grazing regimes, documented since the 1970s. Source: Otterman, Science 1974, 'Baring high-albedo soils by overgrazing'; Landsat archive.
Australia's 5,600 km Dingo Fence has changed the vegetation on either side, and the difference is visible in 32 years of Landsat data. Source: UNSW Sydney, Landscape Ecology 2021.
At night North Korea is almost completely dark between brightly lit China and South Korea. Source: NASA ISS photo ISS038-E-38416 (January 2014); NASA Black Marble.

A desert split by cattle and goats: the Israel–Egypt brightness line.
A fence that rewired an ecosystem: Australia's Dingo Fence seen from orbit.
Finale: the darkest border on Earth, where a whole country disappears at night.

candidates.title: The Places on Your Map That Never Existed
candidates.premise: For centuries, maps carried islands, mountain ranges and even a whole continent that weren't there, and some lasted into the Google era. We hunt them down from oldest to strangest. The finale is a fake town, invented to catch map thieves, that became a real place.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone trusts maps completely. Learning that a 24 km island sat on Google Earth until 2012 and that a fake town became real breaks that trust in a fun, shareable way.
killer_facts: Sandy Island, about 24 km long, appeared on nautical charts and Google Earth until November 2012. Scientists on RV Southern Surveyor found about 1,400 m of open ocean where it should have been. Source: Seton et al., Eos 2013.
Hy-Brasil, a round island west of Ireland, appeared on maps from 1325 until 1865. Source: Wikipedia 'Brasil (mythical island)'; Dulcert chart of 1325.

California was drawn as an island on European maps for over a century, until Spain's King Ferdinand VI decreed in 1747 that it was not one. Sources: Library of Congress / Stanford 'California as an Island' map collections.

The 'Mountains of Kong', a range across West Africa, appeared on maps from 1798 (James Rennell) until Louis-Gustave Binger showed in 1889 that they didn't exist. Source: Bassett & Porter, Journal of African History 1991.

Isla Bermeja appears on Mexican maps, but a 2009 survey found no trace of it. Its existence would have affected how the oil-rich Gulf of Mexico seabed is divided. Source: Wikipedia 'Bermeja'; UNAM/Mexican Navy 2009 survey reports.

Agloe, New York, was a fake town placed on a 1930s map as a copyright trap. Someone later built the 'Agloe General Store' there, and it appeared on Google Maps decades later. Sources: Library of Congress 'Geography and Map Division' blog; NPR.

candidates.title: The Amazon Isn't Earth's Lungs. The Sahara Keeps It Alive
candidates.premise: Almost everyone has heard that the Amazon makes 20% of the oxygen we breathe. It doesn't. The forest's net oxygen output is roughly zero. The real story is stranger: the world's biggest rainforest is fertilised by the world's biggest desert. It pumps more water into the sky than its own river carries to the sea, it starts its own rainy season, and much of the dust that feeds it comes from a giant lake that dried up thousands of years ago. One myth gets busted, and four deeper layers open up behind it, all drawn across one map arc from Chad to Brazil.
candidates.universal_hook: Every person breathes and has been told 'the Amazon gives you 1 in 5 breaths' (it went viral during the 2019 fires). 'So where does my oxygen actually come from?' is a question anyone with lungs wants answered. A desert keeping a jungle alive sounds made up, and it is real.
killer_facts: The Amazon's net effect on atmospheric oxygen is about zero. The '20%' figure is a misreading of its share of land photosynthesis (Yadvinder Malhi, Oxford; National Geographic 2019).

NASA CALIPSO lidar (Yu et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2015): about 182 million tons of Saharan dust cross 15°W each year, and 27.7 million tons fall on the Amazon basin (about 104,908 semi-trucks). They carry about 22,000 tons of phosphorus, roughly what rain and floods wash out.

The Bodélé Depression in Chad, the dried bed of ancient Lake Mega-Chad, is the single largest dust source on Earth (Koren et al., Environmental Research Letters 2006). Fossil lake diatoms literally fly to Brazil.
Amazon trees release about 20 billion tonnes of water vapour a day, more than the about 17 billion tonnes the Amazon River discharges. These are the 'flying rivers' (Antonio Nobre / INPE).
The rainforest starts its own wet season 2-3 months before the ocean monsoon arrives, by pumping moisture through its leaves (Wright et al., PNAS 2017).

At least half of Earth's oxygen comes from ocean plankton. Prochlorococcus, a microbe only discovered in the 1980s, is credited with up to about 20% of the biosphere's oxygen (NOAA Ocean Service; Chisholm lab, MIT).
escalation_arc: Cold open: the viral 2019 claim that the burning Amazon is '20% of your oxygen'. Then the reveal that its net contribution is about zero, and why.
So who makes your oxygen? The ocean. One invisible microbe, discovered barely 40 years ago, may make about 1 in 5 breaths.

Paradox: the Amazon's soil is nutrient-starved and the rain keeps washing phosphorus away. So how is it the greenest place on Earth? Satellites found a river of dust crossing the Atlantic: 27.7 million tons a year.
Trace the dust to its source, one spot in Chad: the Bodélé Depression, the dried bed of Lake Mega-Chad. A dead lake from the Green Sahara is fertilising a living forest 8,000 km away.
The forest fights back. It pumps about 20 billion tonnes of water into the sky every day, more than the Amazon River itself, creating 'flying rivers' that water farms and cities across South America.
It even switches on its own rainy season months early. The forest is not a pair of lungs. It is a weather machine.

Twist: Saharan dust also suppresses Atlantic hurricanes, and marine sediment cores show the dust dropped sharply when the Sahara was green (McGee et al. 2013). The jungle's lifeline depends on the desert staying dead.
Finale: desert, ocean, sky and forest are one connected organism. The real 'lungs of the Earth' fit in a drop of seawater.

candidates.title: The Countries That Are Secretly Getting Bigger
candidates.premise: Myth: the world map is finished. Land is fixed, and if anything is changing, coastlines are only shrinking. Truth: satellites show huge areas of water turning into land. Countries grow from imported sand, from brand-new volcanic islands, from bedrock still rising after the ice age, and from continents literally tearing open. Each method is more dramatic than the last, and it ends with a new ocean being born in Africa.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone assumes the world map is settled and the shapes on the wall are permanent. 'Wait, my country might be bigger than last year?' works for anyone who has ever looked at a map, and the before/after satellite visuals hit instantly with no context needed.
killer_facts: Thirty years of Landsat data showed about 173,000 km² of water became land and about 115,000 km² of land became water from 1985 to 2015. Coasts gained 33,700 km² while losing about 20,100 km² (Donchyts et al., Nature Climate Change 2016, Deltares Aqua Monitor).

Singapore's land area has grown by roughly 25% since the 1960s (about 580 km² to about 735 km²), largely with imported sand (Singapore government land data). The Netherlands' Flevoland is the largest artificial island on Earth (about 970 km²).

Surtsey rose out of the Atlantic in 1963 and is now a UNESCO site. Tonga's Hunga Tonga-Hunga Ha'apai island formed in 2014-15, then was largely destroyed in the 2022 eruption (NASA Earth Observatory).

Finland and Sweden are still rising about 8-9 mm/yr after the ice age. The Kvarken archipelago gains about 1 km² of new land a year, and the two countries are projected to be joined by land in about 2,000-2,500 years (UNESCO World Heritage nomination).

In 2005 a 60-km-long rift tore open in Ethiopia's Afar region within weeks, the start of a future ocean splitting Africa (Wright et al., Nature 2006). Iceland widens about 2 cm a year along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (USGS).
escalation_arc: Cold open: a Landsat time-lapse of a coastline marching into the sea. 'Your world map is already out of date.'
Humans make land: Singapore +25%, the Palm Jumeirah, and Flevoland, the largest human-made island on Earth, built on former seabed.
The satellite census: 30 years of Landsat show coasts gained more land than they lost, overturning the 'only shrinking' assumption.
The planet makes land: Surtsey born from the ocean in 1963, Nishinoshima swallowing its parent island, Hunga Tonga's new island and its violent end in 2022.
Countries rising out of the sea: Scandinavia's bedrock springing back after the ice sheet melted. Finland gains land every year without a single shovel.
Countries being torn wider: Iceland stretching about 2 cm a year, so you can stand between two continents.
Finale: the 2005 Afar rift. Africa is cracking open, and one day the map will show a new ocean. Every map you have ever owned is a snapshot of a moving planet.

candidates.title: The Moon Is Inside Earth's Atmosphere (And It's Rusting)
candidates.premise: Myth: Earth ends about 100 km up, where space begins, and our planet is a sealed ball. Truth: space dust falls into your gutters, and Earth leaks kilograms of gas into space every second. Earth's faint hydrogen atmosphere stretches 630,000 km, well past the Moon, so no astronaut has ever truly left it. Earth's own oxygen reaches the Moon and may be rusting it, and a 4-billion-year-old piece of Earth has been found in a Moon rock.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone has looked up at the Moon and assumed it sits out in empty space. Learning that it orbits inside our atmosphere, that our air is rusting it, and that space dust is on their own roof is the 'that can't be true' reaction the channel was built on.
killer_facts: SOHO's SWAN instrument shows Earth's hydrogen geocorona extends to about 630,000 km, about 50 Earth diameters, past the Moon's orbit (Baliukin et al., JGR Space Physics 2019; ESA).

About 5,200 tonnes of cosmic dust reach Earth's surface every year (Rojas et al., Earth and Planetary Science Letters 2021). Micrometeorites have been recovered from city rooftop gutters in Oslo, Paris and Berlin (Genge et al., Geology 2017).
Earth leaks about 3 kg of hydrogen and about 50 g of helium into space every second (Catling & Zahnle, Scientific American 2009), so the planet is a net mass loser.

Japan's Kaguya orbiter detected oxygen ions from Earth's upper atmosphere reaching the Moon while it passes through Earth's magnetotail (Terada et al., Nature Astronomy 2017). Hematite (rust) concentrated at high latitudes on the Moon's near side may be the result (Li et al., Science Advances 2020; a hypothesis, flagged as such).

Apollo 14 sample 14321 ('Big Bertha') contains a fragment that likely formed on Earth about 4 billion years ago, possibly one of the oldest Earth rocks known, and it was found on the Moon (Bellucci et al., EPSL 2019).
The geocorona was first photographed from the lunar surface by George Carruthers' far-ultraviolet camera on Apollo 16 in 1972 (NASA, public domain image).
escalation_arc: Myth setup: the 100-km Kármán line is a convention, not a wall. Where does Earth actually end?
Space is falling on you: thousands of tonnes of cosmic dust a year, and micrometeorites in city rooftop gutters.
Earth is leaking: kilograms of hydrogen escape every second. Is the planet getting heavier or lighter? Lighter.
Where does it go? A glowing hydrogen halo photographed from the Moon by Apollo 16 in 1972.
2019: the halo reaches 630,000 km. The Moon orbits inside Earth's atmosphere, and every Moon mission so far stayed within it.
Earth's breath reaches the Moon: oxygen carried along the magnetotail, and rust appearing where it shouldn't.
Finale: a piece of Earth about 4 billion years old found inside a Moon rock. The boundary between 'Earth' and 'space' was never real.

candidates.title: There Isn't One North Pole. There Are Five, All Moving
candidates.premise: Myth: the North Pole is one fixed spot at the top of the globe, and your compass points to it. Truth: there are at least five 'north poles'. The one your compass follows has crossed from Canada toward Siberia. The pole star is temporary. The planet's spin axis wobbles, and humans have measurably pushed it. Earth's magnetic field has collapsed and flipped before. The finale: the whole outer planet has tipped over relative to its spin axis.
candidates.universal_hook: Every child learns 'the North Pole' as a single fixed point and every phone has a compass. Being told the north your phone shows is moving about 35-55 km a year, and that people tilted the planet by pumping water, is unsettling enough that anyone wants to know more.
killer_facts: The north magnetic pole has moved more than 2,000 km since James Clark Ross located it in 1831, peaking near 55 km/yr. It forced an unscheduled World Magnetic Model update in 2019 (NOAA NCEI / British Geological Survey). Tampa International Airport had to renumber runways in 2011 due to magnetic drift (FAA).
Polaris is a temporary pole star. Because of axial precession (about 25,800-year cycle), Thuban was the pole star when the pyramids were built, and Vega will be in about 12,000 years (NASA).

Pumping about 2,150 billion tons of groundwater between 1993 and 2010 shifted Earth's rotational pole by about 80 cm (Seo et al., Geophysical Research Letters 2023). Melting ice turned the pole's drift toward England after 2000 (Adhikari & Ivins, Science Advances 2016; NASA JPL).
The 2011 Japan earthquake shifted Earth's figure axis about 17 cm and shortened the day by about 1.8 microseconds (NASA JPL, R. Gross).

About 41,000 years ago, during the Laschamp excursion, Earth's magnetic field weakened to a few percent and briefly reversed (Cooper et al., Science 2021). The south magnetic pole has already wandered off Antarctica into the ocean (BGS).

Paleomagnetic evidence suggests the entire solid Earth rotated about 12° relative to its spin axis about 84 million years ago ('true polar wander', Nature Communications 2021, Italian limestone record; cite carefully).
escalation_arc: Pole #1, Geographic: no land, just drifting sea ice. A flag planted there is carried away.
Pole #2, Magnetic: the one your compass follows, racing from Canada toward Siberia. The 2019 emergency map update, and airports renumbering runways.
Poles #3 and #4, Geomagnetic and Inaccessibility: the 'theoretical' pole and the hardest point to reach in the Arctic Ocean.
Pole #5, Celestial: the pole star changes. The Egyptians had a different one, and our descendants will have Vega.
Even pole #1 moves. The spin axis wobbles in a 433-day spiral, and since 2000 melting ice has steered it toward England.
Humans did this: groundwater pumping moved the pole about 80 cm, and one earthquake moved it 17 cm and shortened the day.
The magnetic field itself fails: the Laschamp event 41,000 years ago, and the weak spot over the South Atlantic today.
Finale: true polar wander. The whole planet's shell tipped about 12°. 'North' is not a place, it is a moment.

candidates.title: The Ground Under You Rises Every Day. Literally.
candidates.premise: Myth: the ground is solid and still, and your home has fixed coordinates. Truth: the Moon lifts entire continents tens of centimetres twice a day. Australia drifted so far that its official coordinates had to be rewritten by 1.8 m. Land rises when droughts lift water off it. Whole regions are still rebounding from the ice age while megacities sink. In the finale, humans moved Earth's axis.
candidates.universal_hook: Every human stands on the ground and trusts that it is still. 'You go up and down like a boat twice a day and never notice' is a universal, personal hook, and the CERN proof makes it believable.
killer_facts: CERN's 26.7 km LEP particle collider measured beam-energy changes that followed the Moon: Earth tides stretched the ring's circumference by about 1 mm (CERN LEP energy-calibration papers, 1990s).
The solid Earth tide raises and lowers the ground twice daily by tens of centimetres. The semidiurnal amplitude can reach about 55 cm at the equator (standard geodesy / IERS tide models).
Australia moves about 7 cm/yr. Its official datum (GDA2020) shifted all coordinates by about 1.8 m (Geoscience Australia).
The 2013-14 drought removed so much water that the western US rose by an average of 4 mm, and up to 15 mm in California's mountains (Borsa et al., Science 2014).

Groundwater pumping moved Earth's rotational pole by about 80 cm from 1993 to 2010 (Seo et al., GRL 2023). The 2011 Tōhoku quake moved Honshu about 2.4 m east (USGS) and shortened the day by about 1.8 μs (NASA JPL).
The Greenwich meridian line tourists stand on is about 102 m from the true 0° of modern GPS (Malys et al., Journal of Geodesy 2015). This is used only as a quick beat because it is already covered.
escalation_arc: Cold open: particle physicists at CERN noticed their 27-km machine was being stretched by the Moon.

Even the zero line moved: Greenwich's famous meridian is about 102 m off true 0°.
The land breathes: drought lifted California's mountains, and monsoon water pushes land down.
Countries rising and cities sinking: Hudson Bay and Scandinavia still rebounding from the ice age while parts of Mexico City sink tens of centimetres a year (InSAR / NISAR).
Finale: humans moved the planet. Pumped groundwater tilted Earth's pole about 80 cm, and one earthquake shifted the axis and shortened the day.

candidates.title: Every Geography Record You Learned in School Is Wrong
candidates.premise: The superlatives on every classroom wall (tallest mountain, biggest desert, lowest land, longest river, biggest waterfall, biggest river) are wrong or incomplete. Each correct answer is stranger and more hidden than the last: summits made of seafloor, a canyon deeper than the Dead Sea buried under ice, a waterfall nobody can see, and a 'river' with roughly 100 times the flow of all rivers combined.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone memorised these records in school and still uses them in trivia. Being told 'you were taught wrong' about every single one is irresistible, and the list format gives a built-in reason to watch to the end.
killer_facts: Chimborazo's summit is about 2 km farther from Earth's centre than Everest's (about 6,384.4 vs about 6,382.3 km) because of the equatorial bulge (NOAA Ocean Service). Mauna Kea rises more than 10,000 m from its base on the seafloor (USGS).

Everest's summit is marine limestone, ancient seafloor with fossils of sea creatures (Qomolangma Formation, Ordovician). River-capture erosion has also boosted it 15-50 m (Han et al., Nature Geoscience 2024).

The deepest land canyon is under Antarctic ice: the Denman Glacier trough reaches about 3,500 m below sea level, compared with about 430 m at the Dead Sea (Morlighem et al., Nature Geoscience 2020, BedMachine Antarctica).
The world's largest waterfall is underwater: the Denmark Strait cataract drops about 3,505 m with about 5 million m³/s of flow, roughly 2,000 Niagaras (NOAA Ocean Service).

The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries about 173 million m³/s (Donohue et al., GRL 2016), on the order of 100 times all the world's rivers combined. Atmospheric rivers carry about 7.5-15 times the Mississippi's flow (NOAA).

Hottest place: satellites recorded land-surface temperatures of about 80.8 °C in Iran's Lut Desert (MODIS-based study, BAMS 2021). Largest desert: Antarctica (about 14 million km²), not the Sahara (about 9.2 million km²).
escalation_arc: Tallest mountain: Everest only by one definition. Mauna Kea is tallest base to peak, and Chimborazo is closest to space.
Plot twist on Everest: its summit is seafloor, and it is still being pushed up.
Biggest and hottest: the largest desert is frozen, and the hottest ground on Earth is in Iran, not Death Valley.
Lowest land: not the Dead Sea, but a canyon 3.5 km below sea level hidden under Antarctic ice.
Longest river: the Nile vs Amazon fight that scientists still haven't settled. It depends on where a river 'starts'.
Biggest waterfall: underwater and invisible. It falls 3.5 km and carries about 2,000 Niagaras.
Finale, the biggest river on Earth isn't a river: the ocean current circling Antarctica, and the rivers in the sky. The greatest records on the planet are the ones nobody can see.

candidates.title: The Earth Rang Like a Bell for 9 Days. No One Heard It
candidates.premise: Myth: the planet is silent and solid, and even the loudest sound fades within miles. Truth: some sounds have circled the entire Earth. Scientists found a brand-new volcano and a hidden mega-tsunami purely by listening. The whole planet rings like a bell after big quakes, and it hums constantly, right now. This is a sonic story where viewers hear real, sped-up planetary signals.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone is drawn to mysterious sounds ('what was that noise?'). A signal that pulsed through the whole planet every 92 seconds for nine days, with no one knowing why, is a true-mystery hook with a satisfying solution. It also directly answers the brief's 'sonically gripping' requirement.
killer_facts: September 2023: a 92-second (10.88 mHz) seismic signal was recorded worldwide for 9 days. It came from a rock-ice avalanche of about 25 million m³ in Greenland's Dickson Fjord, which caused a 200-m tsunami sloshing back and forth unseen (Svennevig et al., Science 2024).

Krakatoa 1883 was heard about 4,800 km away on Rodrigues Island. Barometers worldwide recorded its pressure wave passing up to 7 times over about 5 days (Royal Society Krakatoa Committee report, 1888).
The 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption sent a pressure (Lamb) wave around the globe at least 4 times, and it was audible in Alaska about 10,000 km away (Matoza et al., Science 2022).

A mysterious global seismic 'hum' in November 2018 led to the discovery of a brand-new volcano about 820 m tall off Mayotte, the largest active submarine eruption ever documented (Feuillet et al., Nature Geoscience 2021).

The 2004 Sumatra-Andaman quake made the entire planet vibrate by up to about 1 cm, ringing for weeks (Park et al., Science 2005). Even on quiet days Earth 'hums' in free oscillations excited by ocean waves (Nawa et al. 1998; Rhie & Romanowicz, Nature 2004).
Myth busted: the famous 1997 'Bloop', blamed on a sea monster, was identified by NOAA as an icequake.
escalation_arc: Myth bust: the 'Bloop' sea monster was an iceberg cracking. But the instruments that heard it are listening to the whole planet.
Krakatoa 1883: heard 4,800 km away, with its pressure wave lapping the Earth again and again on barometers.
Tonga 2022: satellites watched the shockwave ring expand around the globe at least 4 times, raising sea levels oceans away.
Mayotte 2018: a hum no one felt led to a volcano no one knew existed, 820 m tall, born on the seafloor.
Greenland 2023: a 9-day planetary heartbeat, traced to a skyscraper-high tsunami trapped in a fjord no one saw. Then it happened again a month later.
Sumatra 2004: the entire planet rang like a struck bell for weeks.
Finale: the Earth's hum. Even now, with no earthquake anywhere, the planet is ringing. We let viewers hear it.

candidates.title: There's a Dead Planet Buried Inside the Earth
candidates.premise: Myth: Earth's interior is the neat textbook onion of crust, mantle and core, and we basically know what's down there. Truth: we have drilled 0.2% of the way. Everything else comes from earthquake echoes, and those echoes revealed a core as hot as the Sun's surface that has reversed direction relative to us, a separate core inside the core, ocean-scale water locked in crystals, and two continent-sized blobs that may be the remains of the planet that collided with Earth and created the Moon.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone has wondered what is under their feet, and everyone saw the onion diagram in school. 'There may be another planet buried inside ours' is an instantly shareable, imagination-grabbing claim with real peer-reviewed backing.
killer_facts: The deepest hole ever drilled (Kola, 12,262 m) reaches only about 0.2% of the way to Earth's centre. All deeper knowledge comes from seismic waves. Inge Lehmann discovered the solid inner core in 1936 from 'impossible' echoes.
The inner core is roughly 5,400-6,000 °C, comparable to the Sun's surface (Anzellini et al., Science 2013).
Seismic repeats show the inner core slowed and began 'backtracking' relative to the mantle around 2010 (Wang/Vidale et al., Nature 2024; Yang & Song, Nature Geoscience 2023).
There is a distinct 'innermost inner core' about 650 km across (Pham & Tkalčić, Nature Communications 2023).
A diamond from Brazil contained ringwoodite with about 1.5% water, suggesting the mantle transition zone may hold ocean-scale water (Pearson et al., Nature 2014).
Two continent-sized low-velocity blobs (LLSVPs) under Africa and the Pacific may be buried remnants of Theia, the Mars-sized world whose impact formed the Moon (Yuan et al., Nature 2023).
escalation_arc: Myth: the onion diagram. Reality check: our deepest hole is a pinprick. So how do we know anything?
Listening to earthquakes: Inge Lehmann's 1936 discovery of a solid ball hidden in the liquid core.
That ball is about as hot as the Sun's surface, yet solid.
It has reversed direction relative to the mantle since about 2010, and it nudges the length of our day.
Inside the core is another core, a fossil of the early Earth.
Ocean-scale water may be locked inside crystals deep in the mantle, found inside a single diamond.
Finale: two blobs bigger than continents under Africa and the Pacific, possibly the corpse of Theia. Every time you see the Moon, you are seeing the other half of that collision.

candidates.title: The Great Wall Isn't Visible From Space. This Is.
candidates.premise: Myth: the Great Wall of China is the one human-made thing you can see from space (it is still repeated in classrooms and quizzes). Truth: from orbit it is practically invisible to the naked eye. But other things are: plastic seas, a mine, artificial islands, a country that goes dark at night. Then we keep climbing, from the ISS to the Moon to Mars to Saturn to Voyager, and humanity disappears step by step until all of us fit inside a fraction of a pixel.
candidates.universal_hook: Practically everyone has heard the Great Wall claim. 'What can you actually see from space?' is a question every person has asked, and the zoom-out ending to the Pale Blue Dot gives the emotional payoff that drives completion and shares.
killer_facts: China's first astronaut, Yang Liwei (2003), said he could not see the Great Wall from orbit. The wall is only about 5-8 m wide and close in colour to its surroundings, far below naked-eye resolution from about 400 km (NASA Earth Observatory).
The idea predates spaceflight: it appeared in print long before anyone went to orbit (for example, Ripley's Believe It or Not, 1932, claiming visibility from the Moon).

What astronauts do photograph: Almería's 'sea of plastic', roughly 30,000+ hectares of greenhouses in Spain (NASA Earth Observatory), plus Bingham Canyon mine, Palm Jumeirah and Saudi centre-pivot farms.
At night from the ISS, North Korea is nearly black between bright China and South Korea (NASA ISS image, 2014). Fishing fleets using lights at sea can outshine cities (NOAA/NASA VIIRS).
From Saturn, Cassini photographed Earth as a dot (2013). From about 6 billion km, Voyager 1's 1990 'Pale Blue Dot' shows Earth as about 0.12 pixel (NASA/JPL, public domain).
escalation_arc: Myth origin: the claim was printed before any human reached space. Then the first Chinese astronaut looked for it and couldn't see it.
Why: the physics of naked-eye resolution, with a to-scale demo from 400 km.
What you can see by day: a plastic sea in Spain, a man-made archipelago, a mine you can see from orbit.
What you can see by night: a whole country in darkness, rivers of light, fishing fleets brighter than cities.
The Moon (384,000 km): every human structure vanishes, and Earthrise (1968) is just a planet.
Mars and Saturn: Earth and the Moon as two dots (Curiosity 2014, Cassini 2013).
Finale: Voyager 1, 6 billion km out. Everything, every border on every map we've ever shown, fits in 0.12 of a pixel.

candidates.title: The First Time Anyone Filmed the Earth Splitting Open
candidates.premise: On 28 March 2025 a security camera in Myanmar filmed what no scientist had ever seen: the ground on one side of a fault sliding 2.5 m sideways in about one second. We use the clip as a doorway into the biggest strike-slip rupture of the decade: a crack running about 475 km, parts of it moving faster than the seismic waves it made, and shaking strong enough to drop a skyscraper in Bangkok, roughly 1,000 km away.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone has felt or feared an earthquake, but nobody had ever seen one actually happen, meaning the ground itself tearing in two. The Shorts that show this clip are already viral (10M and 3.6M views), but no long video explains what the clip shows or why it matters.
killer_facts: Mw 7.7 Mandalay earthquake, 28 Mar 2025, ruptured about 475 km of the Sagaing Fault (other estimates run 470-510 km); average slip 3.3 m, maximum about 5.6 m [USGS publication 'Surface rupture and slip distribution of the 2025 Mw7.7 Mandalay earthquake'; SCEC; Geodesy & Geodynamics 2025]

CCTV about 20 m from the fault and about 120 km from the hypocenter recorded a slip pulse of 2.5 +/- 0.5 m lasting 1.3 +/- 0.2 s (peak 3.2 m/s), along a curved path [Kearse & Kaneko, The Seismic Record 5(3), 18 Jul 2025; Kyoto University release 24 Jul 2025]
Described as likely the first direct video of surface fault rupture during an earthquake [Kyoto Univ. release; Eos 'Video shows pulsing and curving fault behavior', 2025]

The southward rupture ran at supershear speed, faster than the shear waves it produced, though it may have slowed below that near the camera [Hirano, Doke & Maeda, Seismica 2025; CBC News interview with Judith Hubbard]
An unfinished high-rise in Bangkok (State Audit Office tower) collapsed about 1,000 km from the epicenter [AP/Reuters, 28-29 Mar 2025]
escalation_arc: Cold open: a reconstruction of the gate-camera moment. The ground slides 2.5 m in 1.3 seconds, and nobody had ever filmed this before.
Where it happened: India pushing north shears Southeast Asia sideways, and the Sagaing Fault is the seam (3D globe with plate-motion arrows).

The camera was 120 km from where the quake started. The rupture came to it: we animate the crack front running about 475 km, with an overlay showing that distance is roughly Los Angeles to San Francisco.
Supershear: parts of the rupture outran their own shear waves, a 'sonic boom' inside solid rock (wavefront Mach-cone graphic).
About 1,000 km away, soft basin mud amplified the waves and a Bangkok tower under construction came down. How shaking travels across a continent.
The curve: the video showed the slip bending, a fingerprint that lets geologists read the direction of prehistoric earthquakes from fault scratches.
Payoff: the San Andreas is the same kind of fault. We drop a 475 km rupture onto a California map, and the next one will be filmed by millions of cameras.

candidates.title: The Pyramids Were Built on a River That Vanished
candidates.premise: Thirty-one pyramids from Giza to Lisht sit in a strange line along the edge of the desert, kilometers from today's Nile. In 2024, radar satellites that see through sand found the answer: a buried 64 km branch of the Nile, the 'Ahramat' branch, ran right past them. We rebuild the lost river from space and follow it to a 4,500-year-old logbook of boats hauling stone to Giza.
candidates.universal_hook: How the pyramids were built is one of the questions people wonder about most, and 'aliens/lost tech' videos get tens of millions of views. Here a satellite map gives the real, physical answer, and it is more surprising than the myth.
killer_facts: 31 pyramids line a 64 km buried former Nile branch (Ahramat), about 200-700 m wide [Ghoneim et al., Communications Earth & Environment 5:233, 16 May 2024]
Found with radar satellite imagery that sees beneath sand and fields, then confirmed by geophysical surveys and deep soil cores [same paper; UNC Wilmington release; Live Science May 2024]
Pyramid causeways end at valley temples on the old riverbank, which may have been river harbors [Ghoneim et al. 2024]
The branch moved east over time, which may explain why later pyramids sit farther east. Its last remnant is the Bahr el-Libeini canal [Ghoneim et al. 2024]

The Diary of Merer (Wadi al-Jarf papyri, found 2013 by Pierre Tallet) is among the oldest inscribed papyri and logs boats moving Tura limestone to a harbor at Giza in Khufu's 26th/27th year [Tallet, Les papyrus de la Mer Rouge I, 2017]
Pollen cores show a high-water 'Khufu branch' at Giza during construction [Sheisha et al., PNAS 2022]

The 4,500-year-old proof: Merer's logbook of boat trips hauling limestone to Giza harbor.
How the river died (drought, wind-blown sand, eastward drift), and what may still lie buried along its forgotten banks.

candidates.title: We Finally Know What's Hiding Under Bermuda
candidates.premise: We bust the Bermuda Triangle myth with real ship-traffic and accident data, then reveal that the real mystery is the island at its corner. Bermuda is a volcano that went quiet about 30 million years ago and should have sunk, yet it sits on a raised bulge of seafloor. A 2019 study found its lava came from 400-660 km down, and in November 2025 seismologists found a 20 km-thick hidden 'raft' of rock under it unlike anything else known on Earth.
candidates.universal_hook: The Bermuda Triangle is the most famous mystery spot on the map, so curiosity is built in. Paying it off with a real, brand-new scientific mystery satisfies both the myth-lovers and the skeptics.

A seismic study found a roughly 20 km (12.4 mi) thick, lower-density rock layer beneath Bermuda's oceanic crust, about twice as thick as other known underplating, which may hold the island up without a hot plume [Frazer & Park, Geophysical Research Letters, 28 Nov 2025; Carnegie Science/Yale]
Bermuda sits on an anomalous seafloor swell although its volcanism ended about 30 Myr ago, and no hot mantle plume has been found beneath it [GRL 2025 coverage: Discover, Live Science]

Bermuda lavas carry a geochemical signature 'no one has found' in 50 years of ocean-lava research, sourced from the mantle transition zone (410-660 km) [Mazza, Gazel et al., Nature 2019; Cornell release]
That volatile-rich material is linked to slabs subducted around 330 Myr ago, during Pangea's assembly [Cornell / Nature 2019 coverage]

Myth-bust: overlay of shipping and flight density, Gulf Stream and storm tracks. The 'excess' disappears (NOAA/USCG).

The bulge: the seafloor around Bermuda is lifted over a huge area, which usually means a Hawaii-style plume, but there is no plume.
2019: Bermuda's rock comes from 400-660 km down, with a signature never seen anywhere else and linked to Pangea's ancient ocean floor.
2025: one seismometer listening to earthquakes all over the world 'X-rays' the island and finds a 20 km-thick buried raft.
Payoff: Bermuda floats. The real secret of the Bermuda Triangle is under the island, not in the water around it.

candidates.title: Humans Accidentally Moved the North Pole
candidates.premise: By damming rivers and pumping groundwater, humanity has moved enough water around the planet to shift Earth's spin axis by about a meter, and we may also be stretching the length of the day. The chain runs from one dam to every dam, then to groundwater, then to melting ice that now competes with the Moon. candidates.title: What's REALLY Across the Ocean From Your Beach?

The longest straight line you can sail without touching land is 32,089.7 km, from Sonmiani, Pakistan, around Africa and South America to Kamchatka, Russia. Computer scientists confirmed it with a branch-and-bound algorithm, which backed up a viral 2012 Reddit map (Chabukswar & Mukherjee, arXiv:1804.07389, 2018; MIT Technology Review).
The longest straight line on land is about 11,241 km, from near Quanzhou/Jinjiang, China, to Sagres, Portugal, and it crosses 15 countries (same 2018 paper; Live Science).

The Southern Ocean is the only band of latitude (roughly 56-60 degrees S, through the Drake Passage) where you can sail all the way around the planet without hitting land. It carries the Antarctic Circumpolar Current, the strongest current on Earth, which moves more than 100 times the flow of all the world's rivers combined (NOAA; Donohue et al., GRL 2016).

On a Mercator map, 'due east' looks like a straight line. A path that really goes straight across the sphere bends away from it, and that is why the East Coast's ocean view points south of Europe (great-circle geometry, which we can show on screen).

Climax: the longest straight sail on Earth, Pakistan to Kamchatka, 32,090 km (80% of the way around the planet) without touching land, found by an algorithm after a Reddit map got it right first.
