candidates.title: Earth Isn't Round. This Is Its Real Shape.
candidates.premise: Every globe is a lie of simplicity. Measured by gravity, Earth is a lumpy potato. Sea level has hills and valleys almost 200 m apart, you weigh slightly less in some places, the mountain farthest from Earth's center isn't Everest, and humans have changed how the planet spins. A myth-busting tour of Earth's true shape, built from satellite gravity data.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone 'knows' Earth is a sphere. Learning that its real shape is weirder, and that it affects your own weight and the level of the sea, hits every human. It is a myth-bust about the most basic fact we were taught.
killer_facts: The 'sea level' surface (the geoid) is not level. It dips about 106 m below the reference ellipsoid in the Indian Ocean south of Sri Lanka and rises about 85 m near New Guinea and the North Atlantic (NGA EGM2008 / EGM96 geoid models; ESA GOCE mission 2009-2013).
Gravity at the poles (~9.832 m/s²) is about 0.5% stronger than at the equator (~9.780 m/s²), so a scale reads measurably less at the equator (WGS84 normal gravity formula).

The summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is the point on Earth's surface farthest from the planet's center, about 6,384.4 km and roughly 2 km farther out than Everest's summit, because of the equatorial bulge (2016 French-Ecuadorian geodetic survey; NOAA).
Hudson Bay has a measurable gravity low, partly because the crust is still rebounding from the Ice Age ice sheet (NASA/DLR GRACE; Tamisiea et al., Science 2007).

Humans have changed Earth's rotation. NASA calculated that the Three Gorges Dam reservoir lengthens the day by about 0.06 microseconds, and melting polar ice is now measurably lengthening the day (B. F. Chao, NASA 2005; Kiani Shahvandi et al., PNAS 2024).

Myth check, 'smoother than a billiard ball': Everest to the Challenger Deep is about 20 km, or 0.16% of Earth's diameter. On a 2.25-inch ball that is a bump of about 0.0036 in, inside the WPA tolerance of 0.005 in (Phil Plait, Bad Astronomy; WPA ball spec).
escalation_arc: Hook: a perfect blue marble slowly deforms on screen into a lumpy potato. 'This is what Earth actually looks like, and it's not an artist's joke.'
Squashed: the 43 km equatorial bulge, and why Chimborazo beats Everest as the place closest to space.
Myth-bust: is Earth really smoother than a billiard ball? We do the math on screen.
Gravity isn't the same everywhere. Where on Earth you'd weigh the least, and why.
The ocean isn't flat: a 3D sea surface with hills and valleys almost 200 m apart.
Hudson Bay's 'missing' gravity: land still springing back 10,000+ years after the ice left.
The shape changes month to month. GRACE satellites literally weigh disappearing groundwater (India, California's Central Valley).
Climax: humans have changed the spin of the planet (dams, melting ice), and the day itself is getting longer.

candidates.title: How High (and How Deep) Does Your Country Go?
candidates.premise: Everyone knows where their country ends to the left and right. Almost nobody knows where it ends going up into the sky or down into the ground. Starting from the airspace over your backyard, the video goes up to the edge of space (which no treaty defines), to countries that tried to claim orbit, out to the Moon, then down under the sea and into the planet, and ends with one unsettling point: the only place where every border on Earth meets.
candidates.universal_hook: Every human lives in a country and under a sky. 'Do I own the air above my house? How far down does my land go? Where does my country stop?' are questions people have but almost never get answered.
killer_facts: No international treaty defines where national airspace ends and outer space begins. The 100 km Kármán line is a convention (FAI), while the US awards astronaut wings at 50 miles (~80 km) (FAI; NASA/FAA).

In United States v. Causby (1946), the US Supreme Court ended the old idea that landowners own the sky 'up to the heavens'. The case came from a North Carolina farmer whose chickens died in panic when military planes flew over (328 U.S. 256).

In the 1976 Bogotá Declaration, eight equatorial countries claimed the stretches of geostationary orbit 35,786 km above their territory. The claim conflicts with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty ban on national appropriation (Bogotá Declaration text; UN Outer Space Treaty Art. II).
In 2007 a Russian submersible planted a titanium flag on the seabed under the North Pole, about 4,261 m deep, during its push to extend its continental-shelf claim (Arktika 2007; UNCLOS Art. 76).

The Italy-Switzerland border under the Matterhorn was redrawn because the Theodul Glacier melted and moved the watershed line. Switzerland approved the change in September 2024 (Swiss Federal Council; Euronews 2024-09-30).
The China-Nepal border runs right across the summit of Mount Everest (1961 China-Nepal Boundary Treaty).

candidates.title: If Everything on Earth Was Piled in One Place
candidates.premise: Take each category of stuff on Earth and pile it on a real map at true scale: every human, all the gold ever mined, all the ants, all the wild animals, all the water, and finally everything humanity has ever built. Each pile is shocking because of how small or how big it turns out to be. The video ends on the moment human-made stuff began to outweigh all life on the planet.
candidates.universal_hook: 'How much of X is there, really?' is a curiosity everyone has. Seeing all of humanity, or all of Earth's water, as one object sitting on a familiar map gives an instant sense of scale that sticks.
killer_facts: All the water on Earth, gathered into one sphere, would be only about 1,385 km (860 mi) across, roughly the distance from Salt Lake City to Topeka. All liquid fresh water in the ground, lakes, swamps and rivers makes a sphere of about 273 km, and lakes and rivers alone only about 56 km (USGS Water Science School, 2012 illustration; Scientific American).
All the gold ever mined, about 216,000 tonnes, would fit in a cube only about 22 m on each side (World Gold Council above-ground stocks; gold density 19.3 t/m³).

Human-made mass (concrete, metal, asphalt, plastic and so on) passed the weight of all living things on Earth around 2020, at about 1.1 teratonnes. Buildings and infrastructure alone (~1,100 Gt) now outweigh all trees and shrubs (~900 Gt) (Elhacham et al., Nature 588, 2020).
Myth-bust: ants do NOT outweigh humans. About 20 quadrillion ants hold about 12 Mt of carbon, roughly a fifth of human biomass (Schultheiss et al., PNAS 2022).
Of all mammal biomass on Earth, livestock make up about 60%, humans about 36%, and all wild mammals only about 4% (Bar-On, Phillips & Milo, PNAS 2018).

Standing shoulder to shoulder (about 4 people per m²), all ~8.2 billion humans would fit in roughly 2,050 km², less than Rhode Island's land area (our calculation from UN World Population Prospects 2024; National Geographic made a similar LA comparison in 2011).

candidates.title: Every Human Who Has Ever Lived, on One Map
candidates.premise: About 117 billion people have ever been born. Where did they all live, and how many are alive right now? It turns out you're related to nearly all of them, and the ancestor math is so extreme that everyone alive probably shares an ancestor from only a few thousand years ago. candidates.universal_hook: It literally concerns every human: you, your ancestors, the dead, and the living. Questions like 'How many people have ever lived?' and 'Are we all related?' are among the most universal ones there are.
killer_facts: About 117 billion humans have ever been born. People alive today are only about 7% of everyone who has ever lived (Population Reference Bureau, Kaneda & Haub, 2022 update).
Myth-bust: 'more people are alive today than have ever died' is false. The dead outnumber the living roughly 14 to 1 (PRB figures: ~109B dead vs ~8B living).

Everyone alive today likely shares a common ancestor who lived only a few thousand years ago, about 3,000 years ago in the more realistic models (Rohde, Olson & Chang, Nature 431, 2004; Yale/MIT press release).

Go back about 40 generations (~1,000 years) and your family tree has 2^40, about 1.1 trillion, ancestor slots. That is roughly 10 times more people than have ever been born, so the same people must fill many slots ('pedigree collapse', basic arithmetic).

Europeans share a great many ancestors within the last ~1,000 years, which makes descent from figures like Charlemagne close to universal for people of European ancestry (Ralph & Coop, PLoS Biology 2013; Adam Rutherford).
Your next breath very likely contains at least one molecule from Julius Caesar's last breath (the classic Avogadro-number estimate; Sam Kean, 'Caesar's Last Breath', 2017).

candidates.title: Walking Across the Atlantic Ocean Floor, NYC to Europe
candidates.premise: Step off a New York beach and keep walking east on the seabed until you reach Europe. On the way you cross Ice Age land where mammoths lived, drop into a canyon the size of the Grand Canyon, cross the abyss, pass the Titanic, climb the longest mountain range on Earth, and stand in the crack where the planet is tearing open. A first-person journey across real seafloor data.
candidates.universal_hook: 'What would I actually see at the bottom of the ocean?' is one of humanity's oldest wonders. Framing it as a walk the viewer takes makes it immersive and personal, the 'imagine yourself there' kind of question.
killer_facts: The mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, about 65,000 km long, and about 90% of it is underwater (NOAA Ocean Service).

Fishermen have dredged up mammoth and mastodon teeth from the US Atlantic continental shelf. During the Ice Age it was dry land (Whitmore, Emery et al., 'Elephant teeth from the Atlantic continental shelf', Science 1967).

Hudson Canyon, off New York, is the largest known submarine canyon on the US East Coast, with walls comparable to the Grand Canyon's (NOAA Ocean Exploration; proposed Hudson Canyon National Marine Sanctuary).
The Titanic lies about 3,800 m deep, roughly 600 km south-southeast of Newfoundland (NOAA).

The Lost City hydrothermal field, discovered in 2000 near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, has carbonate towers up to about 60 m tall and has been venting for at least 120,000 years (Kelley et al., Nature 2001; Früh-Green et al., Science 2003).

The Atlantic is still widening by about 2.5 cm a year, and only about a quarter of the global seafloor has been mapped to modern standards (NOAA/USGS; Nippon Foundation-GEBCO Seabed 2030 progress report 2024).

candidates.title: Where Does Everything Lost at Sea End Up?
candidates.premise: A message in a bottle, a rubber duck, a sneaker, a LEGO piece, a whole dock. The ocean picks up everything we lose and moves it along hidden highways. Each object's real journey reveals a bigger secret of the ocean, ending with the planet-wide conveyor belt that takes about a thousand years to bring water back.
candidates.universal_hook: Everyone has lost something, thrown a bottle into the sea, or wondered where it would go. 'If I dropped this here, where would it end up?' is a pure imagination question with real, traceable answers.
killer_facts: In January 1992 a container spill dumped 28,800 plastic bath toys ('Friendly Floatees') into the North Pacific. The first reached Sitka, Alaska, about 10 months later, and oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer used them to map currents (Ebbesmeyer & Ingraham; NOAA).
In 1990 the Hansa Carrier lost 61,820 Nike shoes overboard. They washed up from British Columbia to Oregon and helped calibrate ocean-current models (Ebbesmeyer & Ingraham, EOS 1992).
In 1997 about 4.8 million LEGO pieces fell off the Tokio Express near Cornwall, and they are still washing ashore more than 25 years later (Tracey Williams, 'Adrift' / LEGO Lost at Sea project; BBC).

The world's oldest known message in a bottle was thrown from the German ship Paula in 1886 and found in 2018 on Wedge Island, Western Australia, 132 years later (Western Australian Museum; Guinness World Records).
After the 2011 Japan tsunami, about 289 living Japanese coastal species rafted across the Pacific on debris, including a dock that landed in Oregon in June 2012 (Carlton et al., Science 2017).
A flaperon from MH370 washed up on Réunion Island in July 2015, about 16 months after the plane vanished, and its drift was used to analyse the search area (ATSB; CSIRO drift modelling).

candidates.title: Where Was Your Home 300 Million Years Ago?
candidates.premise: Drop a pin on your home and rewind the planet. The ground under New York sat near the equator next to Morocco, Antarctica had forests and dinosaurs, Everest's summit was seafloor, and whales lie fossilized in the Sahara. Your land is still moving today: Australia's GPS coordinates had to be corrected. Finally we fast-forward to where your city ends up on the next supercontinent.
candidates.universal_hook: 'Where was the ground I'm standing on when dinosaurs lived?' is a deeply personal time-travel question every human can ask about their own home. Paleo-globe web tools have gone viral for exactly this reason.
killer_facts: About 300 million years ago, the Appalachians, Morocco's Anti-Atlas and Scotland's Highlands were one continuous mountain range (the Central Pangean Mountains) before the Atlantic split them (USGS; US National Park Service geology).

The summit of Mount Everest is marine limestone (the Ordovician Qomolangma Formation) containing fossils such as trilobites and crinoids. The top of the world was once seafloor (geological surveys of the Qomolangma Formation; Smithsonian).
Wadi Al-Hitan ('Valley of the Whales') in Egypt's Sahara holds hundreds of fossil early whales about 40 million years old (UNESCO World Heritage listing, 2005).
Australia drifts about 7 cm a year, and by 2017 its official GPS coordinates were off by roughly 1.5-1.8 m, forcing a national datum change to GDA2020 (Geoscience Australia).

Antarctica once had forests and dinosaurs, such as the Early Jurassic Cryolophosaurus (~190 Ma) found in the Transantarctic Mountains, and Glossopteris fossil forests (Hammer & Hickerson, Science 1994; USGS/BAS).
Los Angeles is moving toward San Francisco along the San Andreas system. At the plate rate of about 46 mm a year, USGS notes they will one day sit side by side, in roughly 10-15 million years (USGS).

300 million years ago: your city in the tropics of Pangaea, next door to Africa, inside a mountain range that later split in two.

Whales in the desert: the Sahara was a sea.
The top of the world was the bottom of the ocean: Everest's summit fossils.
It's happening right now: Australia's coordinates had to be moved, and continents creep as fast as your fingernails grow.
Los Angeles will meet San Francisco.

ranking.title: Why Do All the Continents Point South?
ranking.why: This has the most universal click in the pool. Anyone of any age in any country who has looked at a globe can see the 'drip', and there is a famous short that proves it: Vsauce's 'Why Does Earth Look Drippy?' has 27.4M views, and Hank Green's version from 26 Sep 2026 already has 2.58M in 5 weeks, so the topic is trending now. For retention, one open loop ('why?') can run the whole video and get answered at about 85%. The middle beats are top-tier sounds-fake facts: dig straight down from the US and you come out in the Indian Ocean, not China; only about 4% of the surface has land directly opposite land; the Pacific is bigger than all land combined; one hemisphere is 89% water. Each is a strong mid-video re-hook. Key finding: I pulled the Vsauce short's transcript, and its answer is 'it's really just a coincidence… apophenia'. That gives us a ready-made reversal ('27 million people were told it's a coincidence. It isn't, entirely.'), which is exactly the '(It's Not X)' pattern that over-indexes in outlier titles (8% vs 2%). The payoff is visual: reassemble Gondwana and the southern tips converge on Antarctica. The finale runs the plates forward to the next supercontinent. Everything renders natively with our globe stack.
ranking.risks: The payoff is the weak point. The honest answer is only partly 'not a coincidence'. The Gondwana pie-slice breakup and the 2022 South Atlantic paper explain the southern tips, but Greenland, Florida, Baja and Korea have separate causes, and Australia tapers north. Overclaim and the comments will tear it apart; be too vague and the people who clicked for 'why' feel cheated. The asymmetry beats (antipodes, water hemisphere, north-heavy population) can feel like a tangent list if they aren't tied back to 'Earth's land is lopsided, and here's why'. The antipodes beat overlaps RealLifeLore's 2.9M video, which is 9 years old. There is a first-mover risk: Vsauce or Hank Green could publish a long-form.
